chapter_theme: The close of the general verses: birth is leaving the Lord's feet to enter the womb-egg, household life is maya's visible form that turns to an old tale, the body is a fortress of ego, anger and lust that no medicine or knowledge can mend and that is fit only for fire. The remedies are the company of devotees, love of Hara's worship, tears before the beginningless one, the guru who takes the poet as his subject, and the two bright feet held within against stone, plaster and copper.
structure_note: The heart (நெஞ்சே) is addressed in 381, 384, 386 and 388, the last closing on the refrain of 361, உனைப்போல் இல்லை பித்தனும். 385 and 387 are the chapter's two verdicts on the body, as useless and as disgusting, and 389 is a closing profession, the poet's own account of what he keeps and what he will not praise.

379.reading: Who weeps for the dung beetle's eggs that fall when the dung is split? Entering the womb-egg you went far from the Feet, and now you fools blubber like people struck by heavy loss; chant every day the name of Hara, which breaks every obstacle and gives release.
379.nuance: எருமுட்டை and கருமுட்டை are set against each other: no one mourns the beetle's eggs, but the human egg (the embryo) is a real loss, since it is the leaving of the Lord's feet. ஒரு முட்டும் வீட்டும் is read as 'breaks every obstacle (முட்டு)' with the pun on வீடு, release; the word play makes the exact sense open. The weeping fools may be mourners at a death or all who grieve.

380.reading: Kohl-eyed wife, sons, livelihood, house: Lord of the red fire, in this world of your maya's appearances in open form, what was real day after day, as the days went by, slowly went away as a plain lie, an old tale, a dream.
380.nuance: உருவெளித்தோற்றம், apparitions in the open, is a term for mirage-like seeing; the household is not denied but reclassified. The three words for its end, பொய், பழங்கதை, கனவு, mark a gradient from falsehood to memory to sleep.

381.reading: Having examined many arts and even gone to the pure great ascetics, you did not learn the truth; on this earth you fell and sank into the lust-disorder of bamboo-shouldered women and stare like a ghost: what madness is yours, my heart?
381.nuance: The heart had the two ordinary means, learning and the company of the holy, and both failed because the question of truth was never asked. பேயாய் விழிக்கின்றனை, staring like a ghost, is the dazed look of the possessed; the same word is used of the ascetic at 363, so possession can be by lust or by the Lord.

382.reading: Apart from the fellowship of devotees, love of Hara's worship and love, is there any gain on this earth? Kin, wife and livelihood, the household Brahma ordained, are like clay pots struck with a stick; yet people have not joined that company.
382.nuance: குயக்கலம் தடியால் அடியுண்டவாறு, pots beaten with a stick, is both the pot that breaks and the potter's own beating of his wares, so the household breaks as it was made to. இனம், the company, is the devotees named in line 1.

383.reading: Treasury of ego, granary of anger, palace that pride never leaves, hall built of lies, high rampart grown to the sky, mansion of lust: this body is a rag; bowing to you fittingly, how is wisdom to bear fruit?
383.nuance: The body is a fortified city, each building a vice. உனைப் பணிந்து is ambiguous: bowing to the Lord in such a body, or bowing to the body itself by serving it; the first makes the verse a complaint that worship in this frame cannot ripen, the second a reproach. கந்தல், rag, undercuts the fortress.

384.reading: Heart that has taken unending births and wandered, sighing and sighing: hear the medicine for the state that does not perish; think in the mind of the beginningless one, the one with axe and deer in his hands, who rides the great bull, let water pour from your eyes, sob and weep, asking only for good.
384.nuance: அவுடதம், medicine, is the Sanskrit word used for the remedy of rebirth; what it prescribes is thought and tears, not a formula. அனாதி here is an epithet of Siva as the one without beginning; the verse's cure is to hold the beginningless in the mind that has a beginning in every womb.

385.reading: Is there a medicine anywhere in the land for a dog's pregnancy? Can a ghost get hold of knowledge? Who would cook or who would eat a great strychnine fruit? Likewise this body: apart from being fuel for fire, tell me what it is for.
385.nuance: Three impossibilities, a cure for what is natural, learning for what cannot learn, and food from what is poison, make the body's uselessness a matter of kind rather than of degree. The verse is not that the body is bad, but that no use can be found for it.

386.reading: Poor heart, who with sidelong glances falling on the heavy breasts in the bodice stands in desire: stitch yourself to the feet of him who shares his side with Unnamulai, the fresh green creeper borne of Himavan; mind, there is never any fault in that.
386.nuance: The remedy for desire for a woman's breast is the goddess Unnamulai (she of the unsuckled breast) at Siva's side, so the verse answers lust with the one female figure it will allow. தைச்சுக்கிட, sew yourself in, is a strong image of attachment transferred rather than removed.

387.reading: I crossed over the glances of deer-eyed women and came; the living guru became my king and settled me in as his subject; there is no fault; whether I go or the gain remains, this good gain is no lie; and even so, staying on in this body is disgust.
387.nuance: குடியேற்றிக் கொண்டனன், settled me as a tenant, is the king's act of resettling subjects on his land, so the guru is a king who gives the poet a place. போனாலும் பேறிருந்தாலும் is hard: whether the poet dies or the attainment stays, or whether he goes away or remains. The last line keeps the body's disgust even after the guru's gift, so the verse holds both.

388.reading: You do not know yourself even a little; you will not fit to speak with those who have examined themselves, even when you reach them; you do not hold the state that is yours; you do not bow to the guru; you went to the harlots and got what you got; foolish heart, there is no madman like you.
388.nuance: Four refusals (self-knowledge, the company of the self-knowing, one's own state, the guru) and one act (going to the courtesans), with the refrain of 361. உனக்கான நிலை, the state that is yours, is the soul's own condition as against what it has taken up.

389.reading: The chiselled stone, the moulded plaster and the copper scrubbed with tamarind until it shines: I do not praise them as fine gold; that keeping the two shining feet within is the truth, I have made known, and shut them in and kept them; henceforth I want nothing else.
389.nuance: The three materials are the three kinds of image, stone, stucco and metal, and the tamarind-scrubbed copper is the processional image polished for the festival. The poet does not say the images are nothing, only that he will not praise them as gold; what he keeps is the feet, held inside and locked.

links.note: Both set the household against its end: the Naladiyar's man sees the corpse carried and the kin wailing yet marries and believes there is joy here, and the funeral drum answers him; Pattinathar's wife, sons and house, real day by day, went away as a lie, an old tale and a dream. The Naladiyar's warning is before the fact, Pattinathar's report is after.

The pot that breaks: Tirumular's potter shapes pots from the tank's clay and people keep the shards of a broken pot but not a broken body; Pattinathar's kin, wife and livelihood are clay pots struck with a stick. In Tirumular the pot is the body, in Pattinathar the household, but both make the potter Brahma's making the reason it breaks.

Pattinathar says the body is fit for nothing but to be fuel for fire; Tirumular says that if a jnani's body is burned the whole land burns with fever, and it should not be given to dogs and jackals. On Tirumular's reading the jnani's body is a thing of power to be entombed, not burned; on Pattinathar's it has no use at all. The conflict holds for the jnani's body, since Pattinathar makes no exception for it.

The Kural says the false embrace of women of wealth is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; Pattinathar lists going to the harlots as the one act of a heart that refused self-knowledge and the guru. Both place the courtesan at the far end from knowing what is real.

Sivavakkiyar asks whether a planted stone will speak while the Lord is within and makes the pot and ladle the whole argument; Pattinathar says only that he will not praise stone, plaster and copper as gold, and keeps the Lord's feet within. Pattinathar's refusal is personal and does not deny that others may worship the image; Sivavakkiyar's is a verdict on the image.

Tirumular once held the body a thing of shame and cherishes it now that the Highest has made it his temple; Pattinathar holds the stone, plaster and copper images apart and keeps the feet inside the body instead. Both move worship inward, but for Tirumular the body itself becomes the shrine, while for Pattinathar (387) it stays a disgust even as it holds the feet.

source_issues: 379 line 1 பிட்கின் is an unusual form, read as பிளக்கின் (when split).
387 line 3 is broken by the line division: பொய்யன்றுகா / னானாலும் should read பொய்யன்று காணானாலும்.
